quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch a platform that lets a company fine-tune a leading AI model safely on its own private data, to a nervous IT director.
quests.correctAnswer: Your own data trains the model inside your own private environment, so you get real AI performance without a single file ever leaving your control.
quests.hint: Lead with the privacy guarantee, since that's the IT director's actual fear.
quests.explanation: For a nervous technical buyer, the guarantee itself is the pitch - the underlying AI method can stay in the background entirely.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch a system that checks an AI's answers for factual accuracy before they reach a business user, to an operations lead worried about costly mistakes.
quests.correctAnswer: Every answer gets checked against the facts before it ever reaches an employee's screen, so a bad guess doesn't quietly become a bad business decision.
quests.hint: Lead with the consequence prevented - a costly decision made on a wrong answer - not the checking mechanism.
quests.explanation: Framing a technical safeguard around the specific costly mistake it prevents makes an abstract reliability feature concrete and motivating.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: The operations lead asks 'what happens on the rare case it flags something wrong?' Answer clearly and honestly, without pretending the system is flawless.
quests.correctAnswer: It gets held back and flagged for a human to check, rather than reaching anyone automatically - better a short delay than a wrong answer going out unquestioned.
quests.hint: Be honest about the imperfect case and what happens then, rather than claiming perfection.
quests.explanation: Answering honestly about an edge case, rather than claiming the system is flawless, is what actually earns trust from a cautious technical buyer.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch a fleet platform that manages self-driving delivery vans for city freight routes, to a logistics operator worried about driver shortages.
quests.correctAnswer: Self-driving vans run your routes around the clock, with no driver shortage and no shift that ever needs scrambling to cover.
quests.hint: Lead with the specific pain - driver shortages - this operator has actually raised.
quests.explanation: Matching the pitch precisely to the pain the listener names, rather than a general benefits list, keeps even a complex technology pitch grounded.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: The operator asks 'what happens if one gets stuck or breaks down mid-route?' Answer honestly and specifically about how that's actually handled.
quests.correctAnswer: It flags the issue immediately and a human dispatcher reroutes the rest of the fleet around it - nothing sits stranded without anyone knowing.
quests.hint: Give a specific, honest answer about the real fallback process.
quests.explanation: A specific, honest answer about a real edge case does more to build trust in an unfamiliar technology than a general reassurance would.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Now pitch that same self-driving van platform to a city council member worried about public safety, using a different angle than the operator version.
quests.correctAnswer: Every route is tested well below the speed and conditions where risk actually rises, and there's a human monitoring the whole fleet in real time, not just software running unsupervised.
quests.hint: Shift the pitch entirely toward safety and oversight, since that's this listener's actual concern.
quests.explanation: The same underlying technology needs a genuinely different pitch for a safety-focused listener than for an operations-focused one.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch a system that lets hospitals share patient data for research without exposing identifiable information, to a hospital's compliance officer.
quests.correctAnswer: Researchers get the data patterns they need, but nothing that could identify an actual patient ever leaves the building.
quests.hint: Lead with the specific guarantee about identifiability, since that's the compliance officer's core concern.
quests.explanation: For a compliance-focused listener, precision about exactly what is and isn't exposed matters more than general reassurance.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: The compliance officer asks 'how confident are we that it's truly impossible to re-identify someone from what's shared?' Answer honestly, including any real limitation.
quests.correctAnswer: Nothing is truly one hundred percent impossible in theory, but the method meets the recognized standard for de-identification, and I can walk you through exactly how it's tested.
quests.hint: Be honest about the limits of any absolute claim, while still being concrete about the real standard met.
quests.explanation: Refusing to overstate an absolute guarantee, while still offering something concrete and verifiable, is more credible to a compliance expert than false certainty.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch that same de-identification system to a hospital administrator focused on research funding, using a different angle than the compliance version.
quests.correctAnswer: This is what actually lets you say yes to research partnerships you'd otherwise have to turn down over privacy risk - funding you're currently leaving on the table.
quests.hint: Shift the pitch toward the funding opportunity this listener specifically cares about.
quests.explanation: The same technical safeguard unlocks a genuinely different value depending on which stakeholder is listening - compliance versus funding.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch a real-time cash flow forecasting tool to a small business owner who's never used financial software before.
quests.correctAnswer: It tells you, today, whether you'll actually be able to make payroll next month - not after your accountant catches up on the books in three weeks.
quests.hint: Translate the technical capability into the specific, relatable worry a small owner already has.
quests.explanation: For a first-time software user, the pitch should skip the category name entirely and go straight to the specific worry it resolves.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: The owner asks 'is this going to replace my bookkeeper?' Answer honestly, clarifying the real relationship between the tool and their existing bookkeeper.
quests.correctAnswer: No, it works alongside your bookkeeper - they handle the official books, this just gives you a real-time heads-up before something becomes a real problem.
quests.hint: Clarify the tool's actual role honestly, rather than overselling its scope.
quests.explanation: Honestly clarifying what a tool does and doesn't replace prevents a misunderstanding that could otherwise undermine trust later.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch the same forecasting tool to that owner's bookkeeper directly, framed around how it makes their job easier rather than threatening their role.
quests.correctAnswer: This isn't trying to do your job - it just means you're not the one fielding a panicked call every time they're worried about cash on hand.
quests.hint: Reassure the bookkeeper their role isn't threatened, and frame the tool as reducing their own workload.
quests.explanation: Pitching the same tool to someone who might reasonably feel threatened by it requires directly and honestly addressing that fear, not ignoring it.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch a gene-editing research project to a funding committee that includes several non-scientists, combining simplification and audience awareness.
quests.correctAnswer: Think of it like fixing a single typo in an extremely long book, instead of rewriting the whole page - that precision is what lets us correct a genetic error without disturbing everything around it.
quests.hint: Use a familiar analogy rather than technical vocabulary, matched to a mixed audience.
quests.explanation: A well-chosen analogy can make a genuinely complex scientific idea accessible to a non-specialist without sacrificing real accuracy.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A committee member asks 'what are the actual risks of getting that edit wrong?' Answer honestly and specifically, without minimizing the real risk.
quests.correctAnswer: An unintended edit elsewhere in the sequence is the real risk - it's rare with current methods, but it's not zero, and any responsible proposal has to say that plainly.
quests.hint: Be honest and specific about the actual risk, rather than downplaying it to seem more fundable.
quests.explanation: Naming a genuine risk honestly, even in a funding pitch, is what separates a credible scientific proposal from an oversold one.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: The committee's lead scientist, who does understand the technical details, asks a more precise follow-up question. Answer with appropriate technical specificity, shifting from the lay explanation you gave earlier.
quests.correctAnswer: Off-target effects are assessed using the current standard screening approach before any edit moves forward, and we'd report those results as part of every phase.
quests.hint: Shift into technical language now that you know this listener can follow it, unlike the earlier lay explanation.
quests.explanation: Reading that the same room contains both a lay audience and an expert, and adjusting language accordingly within a single conversation, combines several earlier skills at once.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch a supply-chain rerouting system to a retail buyer who's never thought about logistics software, focused entirely on what changes for her, not the algorithm.
quests.correctAnswer: When a shipment gets delayed, this finds another route automatically, so your shelves don't sit empty while everyone's still figuring out what went wrong.
quests.hint: Skip any mention of the routing algorithm; describe only the outcome she'd notice.
quests.explanation: For a genuinely unfamiliar audience, the entire technical process can often be skipped in favor of the one outcome they'd actually notice.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: The buyer asks 'how does it even know there's a delay in the first place?' Give a brief, non-technical answer rather than a detailed systems explanation.
quests.correctAnswer: It's watching the shipment the same way a tracking number would, just automatically and constantly, instead of someone having to check it by hand.
quests.hint: Use a familiar comparison - tracking numbers - rather than technical infrastructure terms.
quests.explanation: Comparing an unfamiliar automated process to something the listener already understands, like a tracking number, satisfies curiosity without requiring real technical explanation.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch the same rerouting system to the company's logistics director, who does understand supply-chain systems, using appropriately more technical language.
quests.correctAnswer: It cross-references live carrier data against your existing routing rules and reroutes automatically the moment a delay crosses your defined threshold.
quests.hint: Use the director's real vocabulary, since oversimplifying here would undersell the system.
quests.explanation: The technical audience deserves the technical version - simplifying unnecessarily for an expert can make a sophisticated system sound less capable than it is.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch a customer service AI to a small business owner, deliberately leaving out any mention of 'natural language processing' or similar technical terms.
quests.correctAnswer: It reads what a customer actually typed and answers the way a helpful employee would, any time of day, including nights and weekends you're closed.
quests.hint: Focus entirely on the behavior the owner would observe, with zero technical vocabulary.
quests.explanation: Deliberately omitting technical terms, even accurate ones, is often the right call when the listener needs the behavior explained, not the method.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: The owner asks 'so is it actually smart, or just following a script?' Answer honestly, in plain language, about how the system actually works.
quests.correctAnswer: It's not following a fixed script - it actually reads what's asked and responds to that specifically, though it's not thinking the way a person does either.
quests.hint: Give an honest, plain-language answer without overclaiming or technical jargon.
quests.explanation: Answering an honest curiosity question plainly, without either overselling the technology as fully human-like or dismissively underselling it, respects the listener's real question.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: The owner asks what happens when it can't answer something. Give a clear, reassuring, non-technical answer about the fallback process.
quests.correctAnswer: If it's not confident in an answer, it hands the conversation straight to you or your team instead of guessing - so a customer's never left with a made-up answer.
quests.hint: Describe the fallback behavior plainly, focused on protecting the customer experience.
quests.explanation: A clear answer about the failure case is often what actually earns trust in an unfamiliar AI system, more than any claim about its capabilities.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch a structured investment product with multiple layers of risk protection to a first-time investor, without using terms like 'tranche' or 'derivative.'
quests.correctAnswer: Think of it in layers - if things go badly, the first layer absorbs the loss before it ever reaches your money, like a buffer built in ahead of you.
quests.hint: Use a simple layering analogy instead of financial jargon.
quests.explanation: A layering analogy can make a genuinely complex financial structure understandable without requiring the listener to learn any new vocabulary.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: The investor asks 'so what actually happens to my money in a bad year?' Answer honestly and concretely, without dodging the real risk.
quests.correctAnswer: In a genuinely bad year, you could still lose money - the buffer reduces that risk, it doesn't erase it, and I'd rather you know that going in.
quests.hint: Be honest about the real downside rather than implying the product is risk-free.
quests.explanation: Admitting a genuine possibility of loss, even in a persuasive pitch, is both ethically necessary and ultimately more credible.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch the same structured product to a financial advisor colleague, using appropriately technical language since they share the vocabulary.
quests.correctAnswer: The senior tranche absorbs first losses up to a defined threshold, so investor exposure only kicks in past that point - happy to walk through the actual structure.
quests.hint: Use precise financial terminology, since simplifying here would be unnecessary and could seem to talk down to a peer.
quests.explanation: Matching technical precision to a peer audience, rather than defaulting to simplified language everywhere, is itself part of real audience awareness.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch a warehouse robotics system to factory floor staff who are worried about job security, choosing your details carefully.
quests.correctAnswer: This handles the repetitive lifting that wears people out - it's not here to replace the floor, it's here so nobody's out with a bad back by year three.
quests.hint: Choose the detail that directly addresses the unspoken fear in the room, not a general efficiency pitch.
quests.explanation: When a real fear is present but unspoken, choosing to address it directly - rather than delivering a generic efficiency pitch - shows real awareness of the room.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: A worker asks directly, 'be honest, is this eventually going to replace some of our jobs?' Answer honestly, without dodging the real question.
quests.correctAnswer: I won't pretend the answer's a simple no - some repetitive tasks will shift, but the plan on the table keeps the team, shifting people toward the parts of the job machines can't do.
quests.hint: Give an honest, non-evasive answer, even though it's a hard one.
quests.explanation: A hard, honest answer to a direct question about job security builds more trust than a reassuring dodge, even if the honest answer is uncomfortable.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Pitch the same robotics system to the factory owner, who cares about throughput and safety incidents rather than staff sentiment, using a different set of details.
quests.correctAnswer: This should cut repetitive-strain injury claims significantly and speed up the slowest part of the line, which is currently the actual bottleneck in our output.
quests.hint: Choose details relevant to the owner's priorities - throughput and safety incidents - distinct from the worker-facing version.
quests.explanation: The same system, pitched to two different stakeholders in the same building, needs genuinely different chosen details to actually land with each.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: You need to pitch a company-wide data infrastructure overhaul to engineers, finance, and the CEO, all in one meeting. What's the biggest risk of using one identical pitch for all three?
quests.correctAnswer: At least two of the three audiences will find it either too technical or too vague to actually be persuasive to them specifically.
quests.hint: A single unmodified pitch almost never fits three genuinely different sets of priorities equally well.
quests.explanation: This capstone forces the recognition that real-world complex pitches often can't rely on one script - they need to flex live, within the same room, for different listeners.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: Deliver the core of that pitch in a way that gives each of the three audiences - engineers, finance, CEO - one genuinely relevant sentence.
quests.correctAnswer: For engineering, this removes the fragile system everyone's afraid to touch. For finance, it cuts the recurring cost of maintaining three separate systems doing overlapping work. For leadership, it means we can finally build new things at the speed the market actually needs.
quests.hint: Give each stakeholder group its own specific, relevant sentence within the same short pitch.
quests.explanation: This combines translation, audience adaptation, and message control - naming a distinct relevant consequence for each group in one coherent pitch.

quests.instruction: Deliver the pitch before the lift opens.
quests.prompt: The CEO asks 'what's the actual risk if we don't do this?' Answer honestly and specifically, tying it back to what all three groups have just heard.
quests.correctAnswer: The system stays fragile, costs keep compounding the way finance just heard, and new features keep taking longer to ship - none of that goes away on its own, it just gets more expensive to fix later.
quests.hint: Tie the risk answer back to the specific concerns already raised for each group, rather than a generic warning.
quests.explanation: A strong answer to 'what if we don't' pulls together everything already established for each audience, rather than introducing a new, separate argument.
